pulls.title: 8396408: HSS/LMS key levels are not bounded before signature array allocation
pulls.author: Sovtouch
pulls.body_excerpt: HSSPublicKey reads the level count L from raw and X.509 public-key encodings without checking its range. HSSSignature only checks that Nspk + 1 equals L before allocating arrays sized by these values. A malformed key and a four-byte signature prefix can therefore request very large reference arrays or negative array sizes before the signature body is parsed. Outcomes include memory exhaustion and NegativeArraySizeException. This requires an application to accept the supplied HSS/LMS key and invoke signature verification; it does not imply that every TLS or certificate path uses this algorithm.

pulls.title: 8387067: C2: "assert(C->live_nodes() <= C->max_node_limit()) failed: Live Node limit exceeded limit" for large string concats
pulls.author: 0zzy0sbourne
pulls.body_excerpt: When a method has a very large number of `StringBuilder.append(int)` calls (e.g., 500+), C2's `PhaseStringOpts::replace_string_concat()` can exceed the live node limit because each int append expands into ~150 IR nodes (division, modulo, character extraction). Add a node budget check before expanding each concat: if the estimated cost `(num_arguments * 150)` would exceed the remaining node limit, skip the optimization. pulls.title: 8386509: Avoid creating exceptions if they won't be thrown
pulls.author: raneashay
pulls.body_excerpt: Every time an exception object is created, the constructor calls `fillInStackTrace()`, which has to walk the call stack to record every frame. This is expensive, and it's also unnecessary if the exception is never thrown. There are a few instances in various parts of the JDK libraries where we create an exception in the dominator block but don't always throw it. This patch fixes those cases so that if the exception is not going to be thrown, it is never created in the first place. --------- - [x] I confirm that I make this contribution in accordance with the [OpenJDK Interim AI Policy](https:/

pulls.title: 8378626: C2: Move LoadNodes above loops
pulls.author: merykitty
pulls.body_excerpt: Hi, Currently, a load can only be scheduled before a loop if all of its inputs are before that loop. In this PR, we try to hoist the load above a loop even when the memory input is not a loop-invariant. To do that, we try to analyze the loop, and if all memory accesses in the loop does not interfere with the load, we rewire the memory input of the load to the memory state at the loop entry. This allows the load to be scheduled before the loop. This transformation is performed during the early placement computation of the graph, right after we have built the `IdealLoopTree`. pulls.title: 8373877: QUIC connections are removed too early
pulls.author: djelinski
pulls.body_excerpt: When a QUIC connection receives a CONNECTION_CLOSE frame, it is supposed to enter the draining state, where all incoming (reordered / replayed) packets are silently discarded. However, the current implementation removes the connection from the endpoint, and reordered/replayed packets trigger sending of a stateless reset instead. This patch fixes that issue. I modified the `StatelessResetReceiptTest` to verify that the connection is still registered with the endpoint after it enters the draining state. pulls.author: djelinski
pulls.body_excerpt: > CUBIC is a standard TCP congestion control algorithm that uses a cubic function instead of a linear congestion window increase function to improve scalability and stability over fast and long-distance networks. CUBIC has been adopted as the default TCP congestion control algorithm by the Linux, Windows, and Apple stacks. This PR adds a new congestion controller algorithm. pulls.title: 8370024: HttpClient: QUIC congestion controller doesn't implement pacing
pulls.author: djelinski
pulls.body_excerpt: Implement pacing for QUIC. This is required by RFC 9002. Also, it improves the network utilization on links with long round-trip times. The pacing algorithm itself was created based on the suggestions found in RFC 9002, and on the description of the Linux pacing algorithm. Pacing is enabled when the round-trip time is less than twice the period at which the selector timeout fires. On Linux the selector timeout fires every millisecond, on Windows it's 15.6 milliseconds by default.
